title: Cryptography primer: the four things people confuse

cards.s: Cryptography primer: the four things people confuse
cards.html:
A JWT is not encrypted. It is encoded (so it fits in a header) and signed (so nobody can change it). Anyone can read it; only Laravel can make one that passes your check. If you remember that sentence, you have understood the most common JWT misconception.

To get there, separate four operations that people mix up: encoding, encryption, hashing and signing.

cards.s: Encoding: changing the alphabet, not hiding anything
cards.html:
Encoding writes the same data in a different alphabet so it can travel through a channel that only accepts certain characters. It uses no key, and anyone can reverse it. Morse code is encoding: the message isn't secret, it is just written as dots and dashes so it fits down a telegraph wire.

Why it's needed. An HTTP header is a line of plain text. Raw data can contain bytes that break it: a line break ends the header early, a space or quote can confuse a parser. So the data is first rewritten using only "safe" characters.

cards.s: Encoding: changing the alphabet, not hiding anything
cards.html: Base64 is the most common way to do that. It uses 64 safe characters: A–Z, a–z, 0–9, + and /. Every 3 bytes of input become 4 of those characters, and if the input doesn't divide by 3, = signs pad the end. Base64url is the same thing with two swaps, because + and / mean something special in URLs: - instead of +, _ instead of /, and the = padding dropped. JWTs use base64url.

cards.s: Encoding: changing the alphabet, not hiding anything
cards.html:
Step 1, encode a small piece of JSON:

import base64

data = b'{"role":"student"}'
encoded = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(data)
print(encoded)    # b'eyJyb2xlIjoic3R1ZGVudCJ9'

The result looks like gibberish, but nothing is hidden. Step 2, turn it straight back:

print(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(encoded))   # b'{"role":"student"}'

No password, no key: anyone can do step 2.

cards.s: Encoding: changing the alphabet, not hiding anything
cards.sub: Reading the first part of a real token
cards.html:
The first part of a JWT is its header, encoded the same way. JWTs drop the = padding, but Python's decoder wants it back, so we add as many = as needed to reach a multiple of 4 characters:

header_b64 = "eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IjIwMjYtMTEifQ"

missing = -len(header_b64) % 4          # how many characters short of a multiple of 4
padded = header_b64 + "=" * missing     # put the padding back
print(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(padded))
# b'{"typ":"JWT","alg":"RS256","kid":"2026-11"}'

cards.s: Encoding: changing the alphabet, not hiding anything
cards.sub: Reading the first part of a real token
cards.html: The output reads: "this is a JWT, signed with RS256, using key number 2026-11". That string is the first part of the real ai_token shown in the Laravel team's app guides. Decoding it needed no secret, which is why the guide warns: never log the token, and never treat its contents as private.

cards.s: Encryption: hiding the content
cards.html:
Encryption scrambles data with a key so that only someone with the right key can read it. It is reversible, but only with the key. A locked diary is encryption.

Our JWTs are not encrypted. (There is a separate standard, JWE, for encrypted tokens; we don't use it.) Confidentiality for our tokens comes from HTTPS, which encrypts the whole request in transit.

cards.s: Hashing: a fingerprint of the data
cards.html:
A cryptographic hash function takes any input and produces a fixed-size output (the digest). SHA-256, for example, always produces 32 bytes. Three properties matter:

  • Deterministic: the same input always gives the same digest.
  • One-way: from the digest you can't work back to the input.
  • Avalanche: change one bit of input and roughly half the output bits flip. You can't make a small edit and get a similar digest.

Analogy: a fingerprint. It identifies a person, it's tiny compared with the person, and you can't rebuild the person from it.

import hashlib
hashlib.sha256(b'{"role":"student"}').hexdigest()[:16]   # '...' some value
hashlib.sha256(b'{"role":"admin"}').hexdigest()[:16]     # completely different value

cards.s: Hashing: a fingerprint of the data
cards.html: A hash alone proves nothing about who made the data: anyone can compute SHA-256. To prove origin you need a key. That's where signing comes in.

cards.s: Signing: proof of who wrote it and that nobody changed it
cards.html:
A digital signature is a short value computed from the message and a secret key. Anyone with the matching verification key can check two things at once:

  • Integrity: the message hasn't changed by a single bit since it was signed.
  • Authenticity: it was signed by the holder of the secret key.

The message stays readable. The signature is attached next to it, like a wax seal on a letter: the letter is not hidden, but you can tell if someone opened and re-sealed it, and the seal's crest tells you who sent it.

cards.s: Signing: proof of who wrote it and that nobody changed it
cards.html:
Think of the signature as a checksum that only the key holder can compute. To sign, Laravel does two things:

  1. Hash the message, giving a fingerprint of exactly these bytes.
  2. Lock that fingerprint with its private key. The locked fingerprint is the signature.

To verify, the AI service recomputes the hash of the message it received and uses the public key to check that the signature matches that hash.

cards.s: Signing: proof of who wrote it and that nobody changed it
cards.sub: Why a signed message can't be modified
cards.html:
Suppose an attacker changes "role":"student" to "role":"admin" in a token:

  • The message bytes changed, so its hash changes completely (the avalanche property above).
  • The old signature was made for the old hash, so it no longer matches. Verification fails and the token is rejected.
  • To make a signature that matches the new hash, the attacker would need the private key, which never leaves Laravel. Guessing one is as hopeless as guessing the key itself.

cards.s: Signing: proof of who wrote it and that nobody changed it
cards.sub: Why a signed message can't be modified
cards.html:
The attacker can read and edit the token all they like; they just can't produce an edited one that still passes the check. That's the whole point of signing. A small demo with a shared secret (HMAC, the simpler cousin of RSA signatures) shows the effect:

import hmac, hashlib
key = b"only-laravel-knows-this"
sign = lambda msg: hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()[:16]

good = b'{"role":"student"}'
sig = sign(good)                        # attached to the token

forged = b'{"role":"admin"}'
print(sign(forged) == sig)              # False: the edit breaks the seal
print(sign(good) == sig)                # True: untouched message still matches

cards.s: The comparison in one table
cards.html:
OperationNeeds a key?Reversible?Hides the content?What it gives youIn our system
Encoding (base64url)NoYes, by anyoneNoSafe transport of bytes as textThe three parts of every JWT
EncryptionYesYes, with the keyYesConfidentialityHTTPS (TLS) on every call
Hashing (SHA-256)NoNoSort of, but anyone can hash a guessA fixed-size fingerprintInside RS256: the token is hashed, then the hash is signed
Signing (RSA)Yes, a private key to sign, a public key to verifyNot applicableNoIntegrity and authenticityThe third part of every JWT

cards.s: Symmetric vs asymmetric keys
cards.html:
There are two families of key, and the difference is the heart of why our design is safe.

Symmetric means one shared secret does both jobs. Like a house key: the same key locks and unlocks, and everyone who can get in can also lock up. For signatures, the symmetric version is called an HMAC (hash-based message authentication code). HS256 = HMAC with SHA-256. Whoever can verify an HS256 token can also create one, because it's the same key.

Asymmetric (also called public-key cryptography) means a matched key pair:

  • the private key, kept secret by one party (Laravel), used to sign;
  • the public key, given to anyone (your AI services), used to verify.

cards.s: Symmetric vs asymmetric keys
cards.html:
The maths links them so that a signature made with the private key checks out with the public key, but knowing the public key does not let you compute the private key or produce valid signatures.

Analogy: a letterbox. Anyone can see the slot and confirm it's the real letterbox (verify); only the owner has the key that opens it. Or, closer to signing: a royal seal. Everyone in the kingdom has seen the king's crest and can recognise a real seal (public key). Only the king holds the signet ring that makes it (private key).

cards.s: Symmetric vs asymmetric keys
cards.html:
Symmetric (HS256)Asymmetric (RS256)
KeysOne shared secretPrivate key + public key
Who can signEveryone who holds the secretOnly the private-key holder (Laravel)
Who can verifyEveryone who holds the secretAnyone with the public key
If an AI host leaks its keyAttacker can mint tokens for any userNothing: the public key is public anyway
Key distributionSecret must be copied securely to every verifierPublish the public key at a URL (JWKS)
SpeedVery fastSigning is slower; verifying is still well under a millisecond

cards.s: Symmetric vs asymmetric keys
cards.html: For us, the asymmetric row is decisive. There are four AI hosts (main, V2, chatbot and legacy exam risk), several environments, and multiple teams. With HS256, every one of those places would hold a secret that can forge any user's token, which is the same problem as X-Password with extra steps. With RS256, the AI hosts hold nothing secret at all.

cards.s: How an RSA signature works, intuitively
cards.html:
You don't need the number theory to use RSA safely; the library does it. But a mental model helps.

RSA is a public-key algorithm built on the fact that multiplying two huge prime numbers is easy, while factoring the product back into those primes is practically impossible. The public key contains the product (the modulus, written n) and a small number (the exponent, e, almost always 65537). The private key additionally contains values derived from the secret primes.

cards.s: How an RSA signature works, intuitively
cards.html:
Signing with RS256 (RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with SHA-256) goes like this:

  1. Take the exact bytes to protect: base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload). This is called the signing input.
  2. Hash it with SHA-256. Now you have 32 bytes.
  3. Wrap the hash in a fixed padding format and run it through the RSA private-key operation. The output, the same size as the key (for a 2048-bit key, 256 bytes), is the signature.
  4. base64url-encode the signature and append it as the third part.

cards.s: How an RSA signature works, intuitively
cards.html:
Verifying, which is what your service does:

  1. Recompute SHA-256 of the signing input you received.
  2. Run the signature through the RSA public-key operation. This recovers the padded hash Laravel signed.
  3. If the two hashes match, the token is authentic and unmodified. If a single character of the header or payload changed, the hashes differ and verification fails.
          LARAVEL (has private key)                    AI SERVICE (has public key)
 header.payload ──SHA-256──► hash ──RSA sign──► sig      header.payload ──SHA-256──► hash A
                                                  │      sig ──RSA verify──────────► hash B
 token = header.payload.sig  ───────── sent ──────┘      hash A == hash B ?  accept : reject

cards.s: How an RSA signature works, intuitively
cards.html: This explains test case 7 from the sign-off list: "payload edited (for example role changed to admin)" must return 401. The attacker can decode the payload, change student to admin and re-encode it, which is trivial. But they can't produce a new signature without Laravel's private key, so the hashes no longer match.

cards.s: Why not just check a hash?
cards.html: If the token carried only SHA-256(payload), an attacker would edit the payload and recompute the hash; anyone can. The signature works only because computing it needs something the attacker doesn't have. Remember: a hash proves nothing changed by accident; a signature proves nothing changed on purpose, and who sealed it.
